feeConfigTreasuries.note: FIXED. FeeConfig originally stored the treasury *owner* wallets below, but release_escrow/execute_dispute_outcome require each treasury to deserialize as a Token-2022 TokenAccount — and those wallet addresses did not exist on chain at all, so the entire release path was unexecutable on devnet. The escrow program gained an admin-gated `update_fee_config` (which takes the treasuries as mint-constrained token accounts, so a wallet can no longer be stored where a token account belongs), was upgraded in place, and FeeConfig now points at the settlement-mint ATAs recorded under feeConfigTreasuryAtas. Proven end to end on devnet: scripts/prove-devnet-escrow-release.ts ran a real create-vault -> deposit -> reserve -> create/fund escrow -> approve -> release cycle and asserted the exact 15 bps fee reaching all four treasuries at the 40/30/20/10 split (release signature 5o7Qk11e4yniEzrT8CesCZCCDQf5aVjt1DHCSqNcFqgwZkEz4gp2T1sQNTrnDZTdTSQezt5on3V1f1TUJEqs5tsF). The ATAs are for the devnet settlement (USDC) mint, NOT the OPEN mint: the settlement fee is a slice of the traded amount and is moved by transfer_checked out of the trade's own escrow vault, so treasuries must hold the mint trades settle in. One FeeConfig carries one treasury set, so fee collection currently supports a single settlement mint; a second traded stablecoin needs per-mint treasuries.

stakingAuthorities.note: Corrected by the staking program's new admin-only `update_staking_config`, applied on devnet in 2epNWu1sWqugMLRHwEvof6foAKzR1QZYD5CYeqg8Rxga45upPwcZjGDzRCg2nrkSL16jX7hAkGRNgyoP2e2gRtQK. ONE field was broken, not two. `slash_destination` held HLEB5akyStXEZfsTtgpnzexC4gyvDS5QNiYm1vDSHX4p, an address with NO ACCOUNT AT ALL on devnet, while `slash` requires that key to deserialize as a Token-2022 TokenAccount — so every slash failed at account load and the whole disincentive half of the arbitration incentive was dead code. Nothing rejected the value at write time because `initialize_staking_config` takes it as a plain Pubkey, the same class of defect that made release_escrow unexecutable until update_fee_config fixed it. The new instruction takes the destination as a mint-constrained token account, so neither a wallet nor a nonexistent address can be stored there again, and it rejects a zero authority.
stakingAuthorities.slashDestinationRationale: The emergency reserve owner's Token-2022 ATA for the OPEN mint. OPEN, not USDC: slashed tokens leave the stake vault, which is OPEN-denominated (verified on-chain), so a USDC fee treasury would fail on a mint mismatch. The emergency reserve rather than development or ecosystem because slashed stake is a forfeiture, not earned revenue — routing penalties into an operational budget would give the protocol a budgetary interest in slashing its own participants. [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF] Routing forfeitures to the arbitration pool instead, so honest arbitrators are paid by dishonest ones, is arguably better aligned but is a design change: the pool is a per-case PDA funded by merchant deposits, with no single global account to route to.
stakingAuthorities.rewardsAuthorityNote: EA8TyQ58... — unchanged by this update, and already correct. It does concentrate reward distribution on a single EOA, the same centralisation point crates/rewards documents for the cranker, recorded here so it is a known property rather than a later discovery. Governance-controlled distribution is the eventual answer and is deliberately not this change. Note the program takes both authorities as plain Pubkeys rather than requiring them to sign: a signature would prove at write time that somebody holds the key, but a PDA cannot sign a client transaction, and that rule would foreclose ever handing either authority to a program.

stakingParametersOfs4100.spec: OFS-4100 §4 (signed off), applied to the live StakingConfig singleton 2wrGGjcUFSn1ZiYzo2o64r7ZC88QNhvvgUYktNs2ifT9. Three changes: 500 OPEN floors for Merchant and Arbitrator, a per-role unbonding period, and slash_bps 10% -> 5%.

minStakeByRole.Merchant: 500 OPEN — a FLOOR, not a flat fee. §4 scales the requirement above it with the position taken; the program enforces only the floor.
minStakeByRole.Arbitrator: 500 OPEN — likewise a floor. Down from 10,000.

unbondingPeriodSecsByRole.rationale: Unbonding exists so misconduct discovered after the fact still has stake to bite on, so each role's period tracks how long its misconduct takes to surface. A merchant's failure is visible inside one settlement window and a long lock is a direct cost to liquidity; an arbitrator's only surfaces at reveal-and-tally; everyone else is judged on sustained behaviour over time, so their stake stays exposed longest.

stakingParametersOfs4100.slashBps: 500 (5%), down from 1000. Not leniency about the same offence — a percentage slash of a 500 OPEN floor is a small absolute penalty, and OFS-2400 §16 asks for a 'partial, moderate' slash rather than a figure that makes a minimum-staked arbitrator's first mistake terminal. The real consequence of a slash is losing eligibility: StakeAccount::effective_stake already returns 0 below the role minimum.
stakingParametersOfs4100.whyTheArbitratorFloorCouldBeLowered: It could not have been before arbitrator sortition landed (#118). Dispute seats went to whoever called commit_dispute_vote first, so capture cost seven staked wallets and 10,000 OPEN was the only price on it; 500 would have made that twenty times cheaper. Seat eligibility is now a per-case draw — openfiat_programs_shared::sortition::qualifies_for_seat, enforced by a require! in escrow::commit_dispute_vote — so assembling a majority needs many aged, funded wallets rather than seven of any size. The barrier moved from the size of one stake to the number of independent stakes, which is what a per-wallet minimum could never price.
stakingParametersOfs4100.CAVEAT_sortitionIsOffByPARAMETERonDevnet: The sortition CODE is live in the deployed escrow program, but FeeConfig.arbitrator_sortition_bps is 0 on devnet (read off 6JPUB6RUxgpDPWZqcXhkMYXV8gofMYxwbMfNr8fLAUHX), and zero disables the draw entirely — qualifies_for_seat returns true for everyone. min_arbitrator_stake_age_secs is likewise 0. Both ship inert deliberately (a 30-day age gate cannot be met on a young chain, and a 1/100 draw deadlocks a ten-arbitrator pool), and governance raises them through update_fee_config. Until it does, the 500 floor is protected by code that is not switched on. That is acceptable on devnet, where no seat carries real value; it MUST be switched on before the floor ships anywhere that does.
stakingParametersOfs4100.loweringAMinimumStrandsNobody: Checked rather than assumed. request_unstake enforces StakingConfig::is_legal_balance — zero, or at least the role minimum — against whatever the config holds at the time. Lowering a minimum can only widen the set of legal balances, so no position already open can be caught between the old and new values. (Raising one would leave accounts below the new floor, and they stay exitable because is_legal_balance admits zero unconditionally: a minimum must never be able to trap tokens.) One real consequence in the other direction: accounts a slash had pushed below the OLD 10,000 arbitrator floor counted as zero weight and now count in full again, because effective_stake compares against the live minimum. StakingConfigUpdated carries the whole min_stake_by_role array so that change to the electorate is visible in the log.
stakingParametersOfs4100.layoutChange: StakingConfig held ONE flat unbonding_period_secs, which cannot express §4's three different periods. It became unbonding_period_secs_by_role ([i64; 7], indexed by Role), placed exactly where the flat field was rather than appended — appending would leave a now-meaningless field mid-layout and two sources of truth for one parameter. The account grew 237 -> 285 bytes, so from the moment the new binary was deployed the live singleton no longer deserialized and every instruction loading it failed: stake, request_unstake, withdraw_unstaked, slash, and governance's cast_vote through it. That window is real; it was closed by running the migration in the next command.
stakingParametersOfs4100.migratedInPlace: The account was rewritten IN PLACE by the program's own migrate_staking_config (scripts/migrate-devnet-staking-config.ts), never recreated — the config PDA and both token vaults must keep their addresses, and the stake vault holds real staked OPEN that a new config could not sign for. Same mechanism used when min_stake became per-role. The instruction now takes only the unbonding array: it migrates LAYOUT and never policy, so min_stake_by_role, slash_bps and all three authorities are carried across verbatim and the script asserts afterwards that none of them moved. Policy is written separately by update_staking_config, where it is validated and emits StakingConfigUpdated. A resize that also restated policy would be a parameter write nobody could audit.
stakingParametersOfs4100.decodeDiscipline: OFS-4200 §7.1. Both scripts decode StakingConfig with a single moving cursor and assert the walk consumes exactly the account length minus its three trailing u8 bumps (234 of 237 before, 282 of 285 after). scripts/fix-devnet-staking-authorities.ts was rewritten to the same walk: its per-field offsets would have kept computing after the array shifted every later field by 48 bytes, and would have read every value after the array out of the wrong place. This is the same class of mistake that once produced two adjacent pubkeys with their identities transposed on this exact struct — well-formed, plausible, and wrong. The program carries the matching check as a const assert: OLD_LEN + 8*(COUNT-1) == 8 + StakingConfig::INIT_SPACE, so a field added or reordered without the offsets following fails the build.

stakingParametersOfs4100.nodeStakeImpact: node1/node2 sit at exactly the 1,000 OPEN NodeOperator minimum, which this change does NOT touch — the floors that moved are Merchant and Arbitrator. They remain exactly at their floor with zero slack, as devnet_nodes.stakeNote already records.

governanceForfeitDestination.note: FIXED. GovernanceConfig.forfeit_destination held VueuQemTWZcZXMhfN1jRH1vs1zeWXYvzhDPC8uxJARF — the ecosystem treasury *owner* wallet, not a token account. This is the same class of defect as the FeeConfig treasuries and staking's slash_destination: initialize_governance_config takes the field as a plain Pubkey, so nothing rejected a wallet at write time. The impact was wider than the field's name suggests. refund_or_forfeit_deposit loads forfeit_destination as a Token-2022 TokenAccount in its *account context*, before the handler chooses a branch, so account loading failed on every call — REFUNDS TOO, not just forfeitures. A proposal's deposit could never be settled either way, in either direction. The governance program gained an admin-gated `update_governance_config` which takes the destination as a mint-constrained token account (and additionally requires governance_config.mint == mint, since GovernanceConfig records its own mint), so neither a wallet nor a wrong-mint account can be stored there again.
governanceForfeitDestination.forfeitDestinationRationale: [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF] The ecosystem treasury owner's Token-2022 ATA for the OPEN mint. OPEN, not USDC: the governance deposit vault is OPEN-denominated, so a USDC treasury would fail on a mint mismatch. The owner is deliberately unchanged from the wallet the config already named — the stored value recorded where forfeited deposits were meant to go, so this corrects the type error without quietly relocating protocol income. CONSIDERED AND DECIDED THE OTHER WAY: slashDestination above routes forfeitures to the emergency reserve on the reasoning that penalties should not fund an operational budget, or the protocol acquires a budgetary interest in punishing its own participants. A forfeited proposal deposit is arguably the same class of forfeiture and the same argument applies. It was weighed and decided for the ecosystem treasury for now, on the grounds that deposit forfeiture is triggered by a token-weighted vote missing quorum rather than by an authority with a budget, which weakens (but does not eliminate) the incentive concern. Recorded here so the argument does not have to be rediscovered.

governanceForfeitDestination.decodeDiscipline: OFS-4200 §7.1. The script decodes GovernanceConfig with a single moving cursor and asserts the walk consumes exactly the account length minus its two trailing u8 bumps (138 of 140 bytes). This is not ceremony: an earlier StakingConfig decode in this repo used independently-computed per-field offsets, skipped a 32-byte field, and reported two adjacent pubkeys with their identities transposed — both well-formed, both wrong, and it read as correct until the chain contradicted it. A cursor that must balance cannot skip a field silently. The decoded values are also individually recognisable (5001 bps, 5000 OPEN at 9 decimals, 604800s), which catches a transposition that a balanced walk alone would not.

feeSplitRemainderOfs4100.spec: OFS-4100 §6 (signed off): the remainder from an integer-division fee split goes to the ECOSYSTEM treasury sub-account. It went to the emergency reserve until now.
feeSplitRemainderOfs4100.scope: escrow::instructions::shared_logic::split_fee_four_ways, the single place a fee remainder is computed. Both fee paths route through it — the settlement fee via compute_fee_split (release_escrow and execute_dispute_outcome's BuyerWins arm) and the flat ad-listing fee via charge_ad_listing_fee — so fixing it once fixes both, and they cannot drift apart. Checked that no other fee path computes its own remainder: the only other truncation-remainder in the program is claim_arbitration_reward's, which hands the last claimant the dust left in a per-case arbitration reward pool. That is a payout to arbitrators, not a treasury split, and §6 does not reach it.
feeSplitRemainderOfs4100.whyBotherAtAll: The amounts are sub-unit rounding dust and the value at stake is negligible. The reason to do it is that the spec and the program must not disagree about where protocol income goes. A discrepancy nobody notices is exactly how the FeeConfig-treasuries defect and staking's slash_destination survived as long as they did: nothing was ever compared.
feeSplitRemainderOfs4100.proof: Unit tests in shared_logic.rs pin the arithmetic (remainder to index 1; the four shares always sum back to the fee across 1,000 fee values and two splits). tests/escrow.ts's ad-listing fee fixture was changed to 1 OPEN + 3 base units so 40/30/20/10 of it does NOT divide evenly, and asserts the dust lands on the ecosystem treasury — a fee that divides evenly proves the routing but says nothing about the dust.

settlementMintAllowlist.note: FeeConfig gained a 16-slot settlement-mint allowlist plus a count byte, APPENDED after arbitrator_sortition_bps so the live singleton migrates by a resize alone. Enforced at reserve_liquidity and create_trade_escrow (strictly) and at create_liquidity_vault (with a carve-out, see openCarveOut below). NOT enforced at deposit_liquidity or withdraw_liquidity: de-listing a mint must stop new exposure, not seize balances that are already in a vault.
settlementMintAllowlist.whyItExists: All four programs declared token_program as Program<'info, Token2022>, which made the CPI target a compile-time constant. wSOL and Circle's devnet USDC are both owned by the LEGACY SPL Token program, so the escrow could not hold a single one of the stablecoins it exists to escrow. Every test passed because every fixture mint was created as Token-2022 — the fixtures matched the constraint rather than production. The programs now take Interface<'info, TokenInterface> and every mint carries mint::token_program, which re-establishes 'the supplied program owns this mint' as a runtime check instead of a compile-time one. Once any mint is possible, an allowlist is what stops a look-alike mint being settled against.

Three legacy plus one Token-2022 is deliberate: the list itself then exercises both dispatch paths, rather than repeating the fixture mistake where every mint was Token-2022 and the legacy path was never touched.
settlementMintAllowlist.openCarveOut: [CONFIRMED — protocol steward] OPEN is deliberately NOT on the list (steward: 'Open will be supported once it comes to public sale'), but create_liquidity_vault is ALSO how a merchant's OPEN vault comes into existence — the vault charge_ad_listing_fee debits and open_dispute_case takes the arbitration deposit from. An unconditional allowlist there would have made charge_ad_listing_fee uncallable and silently reduced every arbitration deposit to zero (open_dispute_case takes what the vault can cover and opens the case anyway rather than letting an underfunded merchant block a buyer's dispute), removing the arbitrator reward pool without failing loudly. So create_liquidity_vault accepts an allowlisted mint OR the mint held by the arbitration_pool PDA — a seeds-pinned singleton whose .mint is the program's only existing definition of OPEN, so it cannot be spoofed and costs no new FeeConfig field. The pool is read only on the carve-out path, so a chain without one still creates allowlisted settlement vaults normally.
settlementMintAllowlist.usdtStatus: RESOLVED, not a deviation. The steward's directive named USDT and no devnet USDT existed in this repo; C4rSGhdx... was created for the purpose and is on the list.
settlementMintAllowlist.migrationRequired: NOT YET APPLIED. The live FeeConfig at 6JPUB6RUxgpDPWZqcXhkMYXV8gofMYxwbMfNr8fLAUHX is at 203 or 213 bytes and must be grown to 726 by migrate_fee_config before any escrow instruction gated on the allowlist will execute. The migration accepts EITHER starting length — whether the earlier arbitrator-gate migration was ever submitted is a fact about the cluster, not about this repository, so it is read off the account rather than assumed. It writes the four defaults above; leaving the list empty would take the deployment offline until a second transaction landed, which is why the allowlist migrates POPULATED while the two arbitrator gates migrate DISABLED.
settlementMintAllowlist.clientBreakingChange: reserve_liquidity, create_liquidity_vault and create_trade_escrow all gained accounts, and update_fee_config's params gained a trailing Borsh Vec<Pubkey>. execute_dispute_outcome additionally gained a second token program (deposit_token_program) because it moves the settlement stablecoin and the OPEN deposit atomically and a mint's owning program is fixed at creation — on devnet those two programs genuinely differ. Clients using Anchor's IDL-driven resolution need no change: every added account is a PDA with constant seeds and resolves automatically. Hand-built clients must add them in IDL order. The Rust and TypeScript SDK builders in openfiat-sdks were updated.

disputeParameters.note: Dispute-case parameters introduced with the arbitration security fix. All three are [PROPOSED — NEEDS SIGN-OFF]: they are economic/liveness choices, not values any spec fixes. commitDisputeVote is now gated on the committer holding the Arbitrator role's minimum stake (min_stake_by_role[Arbitrator], currently 10,000 OPEN) — previously any wallet could commit, and since initialize_stake_account is permissionless and a zero balance is legal, seven throwaway wallets could occupy all MAX_ARBITRATORS seats for the price of rent, reveal zero-weight votes, and drive the tally to an all-zero tie that resolved to InvalidDispute, returning the escrow to the seller. A merchant could keep a buyer's money after the buyer had sent fiat. The tally now also skips zero-weight reveals, and an undecided round no longer pays anyone: it re-opens the case, bounded by maxDisputeRounds, after which the escrow splits evenly so neither side profits from forcing indecision. MutualSettlement likewise splits evenly rather than falling into the merchant-wins arm as it previously did; a ratio-bearing partial settlement (OFS-2400 §17) remains future work. minDisputeWindowSecs is deliberately low — it is a liveness guard against a same-block window, not the anti-squatting defence, which is the stake gate; a production floor should reflect real arbitrator discovery latency over gossip.
disputeParameters.undecidedRoundPolicy: re-open the case; split the escrow evenly once maxDisputeRounds is reached
disputeParameters.settlementFeeOnEvenSplit: none — the protocol did not successfully arbitrate

rewardsAndFees.note: OFS-4100 §9 implementation. Three fees with three payers, each now with an identified source of funds: the BUYER bears the settlement fee (deducted from the escrowed amount at release, in the traded stablecoin); the MERCHANT bears the ad-listing fee (charge_ad_listing_fee, debited from their OPEN liquidity vault) and the arbitration deposit (open_dispute_case, also from their OPEN vault, whoever opened the case). Before this, ad_listing_fee and dispute_filing_fee were stored on FeeConfig and read by no instruction, and no instruction funded the staking rewards vault, so no reward was ever payable.
rewardsAndFees.settlementFeeBpsStatus: [DECISION — protocol steward] 0.85%, superseding the 15 bps originally deployed. Governance-updatable via update_fee_config.
rewardsAndFees.arbitrationPoolNote: Singleton OPEN token account owned by the FeeConfig PDA, created by initialize_arbitration_pool. Deliberately NOT one of the four settlement-fee treasuries: those are external wallet-owned accounts routing revenue, whereas this holds funds still owed either back to a merchant or forward to arbitrators. Mixing a liability with revenue would make neither auditable.
proposedNeedsSignOff: Arbitration deposit disposition when the merchant WINS or the outcome is InvalidDispute: returned to the merchant's OPEN vault. The steward specified forfeiture only for 'merchant loses'; 'deposit' ordinarily implies return when not at fault, but this was not stated.

Arbitration deposit disposition at the MAX_DISPUTE_ROUNDS terminal even split (no consensus, no loser): returned to the merchant's OPEN vault. Forfeiting on 'nobody reached consensus' would punish a merchant for an outcome the arbitrators failed to produce.
Arbitration deposit disposition on MutualSettlement: returned, same reasoning — neither side was found at fault.

Partial/zero deposit collection when the merchant's OPEN vault cannot cover the fee: the case opens anyway with whatever was available, and the shortfall is recorded in the ArbitrationDepositTaken event. Requiring the full deposit would let a merchant make themselves undisputable by keeping their OPEN vault empty, which is a far worse failure than one case's arbitrators going unpaid.
Ad-listing fee destination: the development treasury. OFS-4100 §6 sets the fee's amount but names no destination, and splitting a small flat charge four ways would add four accounts to every listing.

Ad-listing fee charged via a dedicated instruction rather than at vault creation, deposit, or reservation: a merchant funds once but lists many times, and charging at reservation would bill per trade, which is the settlement fee's job.
rewardsAndFees.slashBelowMinimumNote: slash may now leave a balance below the role minimum, and deliberately does. Sweeping the remainder to zero would also restore the 'non-zero stake is a qualifying stake' invariant, but it turns a slash_bps penalty into total forfeiture for anyone staked at the minimum — the common case for arbitrators, and contrary to OFS-2400 §16's 'partial, moderate stake slash'. The invariant is instead enforced in StakeAccount::effective_stake, which returns 0 below the minimum, so governance vote weight and the dispute tally both ignore such an account while it keeps its tokens.
rewardsAndFees.eventsNote: The programs workspace previously contained zero emit!/#[event]. Reward, claim, slash, vault-funding, escrow-release (with the full four-way fee split), dispute-resolution, deposit-taken and reward-claim events are now emitted so an indexer can rebuild history from logs alone (OFS-4100 §9.4).

banList.spec: OFS-7100 §12 — the protocol-enforced ban list. A wallet on the list cannot deposit into any vault; enforcement is in the programs, not in each application.
banList.authority: GOVERNANCE-EXECUTED. A passed proposal is the only authority; no key can list or delist. list_wallet/delist_wallet take a finalized Proposal plus the ProposalAction PDA derived from it, and no constraint in either instruction names GovernanceConfig.admin. Execution requires the proposal to have passed, met quorum and cleared its vote lock, and spends it in the same instruction so it cannot run twice. The submitter is whoever pays the transaction, not an authority: a stranger with no standing can execute a passed proposal, which is the positive proof that authority is the vote rather than the sender. The action is fixed when the proposal is created and can never be attached or altered afterwards, so a proposal naming wallet A cannot be redeemed against wallet B. Delisting runs the identical path deliberately — an authority that could exclude but not readmit is the specific failure OFS-7100 §12.2 names. This replaces the previously deployed admin gate, under which one key could deny any wallet deposit access to the entire protocol.
banList.remainingWorkForGovernanceControl: DONE. Proposal execution now exists and both instructions are gated on it. Two residual items, neither an authority over the ban list itself: (1) admin still writes GovernanceConfig.vote_lock_secs. Left unbounded, one key could park it past any horizon and leave every accepted proposal — including one delisting a wallet — unexecutable, which is the same veto wearing a different hat; it is now bounded by MAX_VOTE_LOCK_SECS (30 days) with a test, so the power is bounded rather than removed and admin can still delay any execution by up to a month. (2) Whether banning needs an emergency fast path for an actively-draining stolen-funds wallet is OPEN and unanswered; the deployed behaviour is no fast path, so every ban waits for a full vote. If one is ever added it must be a timelocked multisig with mandatory governance ratification, never a single key.

record.fields: wallet, reason (StolenFunds|Sanctions|Phishing|Scam|Other), evidence_hash, listed_at, listed_by, bump
record.readableOnChain: Yes — §12.2 requires it. reason and evidence_hash are stored so a listing can be audited and contested against a fixed artefact, not just enforced.
record.events: WalletListed on list_wallet, WalletDelisted on delist_wallet — both required by §12.2. WalletDelisted carries the original listed_at, because the record that knew it is closed by the time the event is read.

enforcement.mechanism: Proof of non-existence. Each gated instruction takes the canonical ban address for ITS OWN SIGNER as an UncheckedAccount constrained by seeds = [BAN_SEED, signer], seeds::program = GOVERNANCE_PROGRAM_ID, and requires it to be unoccupied. A wallet is banned iff that address holds an account.
enforcement.whyTheConstraintIsTheWholeProperty: Anchor re-derives the address from the signer's key and rejects a mismatch. Without that, a banned caller would pass any unrelated empty account and the emptiness check would pass them — the gate would be decorative. Two tests cover this directly: an unrelated empty account is rejected, and so is another wallet's real, genuinely-empty ban PDA. Both fail with ConstraintSeeds.
enforcement.sharedImplementation: BAN_SEED, GOVERNANCE_PROGRAM_ID and wallet_is_banned live in openfiat-programs-shared, not in the governance crate. escrow/staking/presale cannot depend on governance — governance already depends on staking to weigh votes, so staking -> governance would close a dependency cycle. The gate needs only two constants because it never deserializes a BanRecord, so the shared crate breaks the cycle and gives all four programs one implementation instead of four hand-copied ones. governance asserts its declare_id! equals the shared constant in a unit test; a divergence would silently disable every gate at once without failing any build.

gatedInstructions.escrow::deposit_liquidity: Merchant ATA -> liquidity vault. A deposit into a vault.
gatedInstructions.staking::stake: Owner ATA -> stake vault. A deposit into a vault.
gatedInstructions.staking::fund_rewards_vault: Funder ATA -> rewards vault. See fundRewardsVaultDecision below — this one is a genuine judgement call.
gatedInstructions.governance::create_proposal: Proposer ATA -> deposit vault. A deposit into a vault.
gatedInstructions.presale::contribute_usdc: Buyer ATA -> presale usdc_vault. A deposit into a vault.
gatedInstructions.presale::contribute_with_swap: Buyer's SOL/whitelisted stablecoin -> presale usdc_vault via a swap CPI. Same deposit through a different door.

notGatedAndWhy.escrow::fund_trade_escrow: NOT GATED, and this is a departure from the original brief, which listed it. Its `from` is liquidity_token_vault — a protocol-owned PDA, not the merchant's wallet. The tokens are already inside the protocol; they entered through deposit_liquidity, which IS gated. Gating it would not stop a deposit, it would strand already-deposited liquidity mid-trade, and it would break a counterparty buyer who had already committed to the trade because of the merchant's status. That is confiscation and collateral damage, not exclusion.
notGatedAndWhy.escrow::charge_ad_listing_fee, escrow::o: NOT GATED. Both debit the merchant's already-funded OPEN liquidity vault (a PDA), not a wallet. Same reasoning as fund_trade_escrow.
notGatedAndWhy.withdrawal and payout paths: NOT GATED: escrow::withdraw_liquidity, escrow::claim_arbitration_reward, staking::request_unstake, staking::withdraw_unstaked, staking::claim_rewards, presale::claim, presale::refund. §12 excludes banned wallets from depositing, not from recovering what they already deposited. Gating these would be seizure of existing balances, which §12 does not authorize and which no delisting could undo if the funds had meanwhile been swept. The Rust SDK carries an explicit test (request_unstake_carries_no_ban_gate) so an accidental gate here fails CI rather than silently seizing.
notGatedAndWhy.authority-driven and permissionless path: NOT GATED: staking::slash (slashing authority), presale::finalize_sale (admin), escrow::execute_dispute_outcome and governance::refund_or_forfeit_deposit (no signer at all — nothing to check a ban against).

banList.gateListVsBrief: The brief supplied five instructions and asked for them to be verified. Result: one removed (escrow::fund_trade_escrow, vault-to-vault, see above) and two added (presale::contribute_usdc and presale::contribute_with_swap). contribute_with_swap is the important addition: it moves funds into the presale vault entirely through a swap CPI and contains no transfer_checked of its own, so it does not appear in a transfer-site inventory at all. Gating contribute_usdc while leaving it open would have left the presale gate bypassable by routing the same contribution through the swap path.
banList.fundRewardsVaultDecision: GATED, and it was close. The argument against: it is a one-way donation. The funder gets no stake account, no claim, no receipt, no position — refusing it denies the banned party nothing they wanted and costs the protocol a donation, so the gate looks like it punishes the protocol more than the listed wallet. The argument that won: accepting it means knowingly taking tokens from a wallet governance has declared stolen or sanctioned and distributing them to honest stakers, who cannot refuse the taint and had no part in the decision. Pushing the contamination onto uninvolved third parties is worse than declining a donation nobody was counting on — realistically the rewards pool is funded by protocol fee flows, not by walk-up donors, so the expected cost of refusing is about zero. Secondary: §12 says 'any vault' without exception, and the rewards vault is a vault; carving out the first exception invites the same argument for the next one. Limitation, stated plainly: the gate is not a laundering defence. A determined actor donates from a fresh unbanned wallet. What it buys is that the protocol does not KNOWINGLY accept from a wallet it has itself listed.
banList.clientBreakingChange: Adding an account to an instruction's Accounts struct changes its wire format. Any client that builds deposit_liquidity, stake, fund_rewards_vault, create_proposal, contribute_usdc or contribute_with_swap by hand must add the ban_record account in the position shown in the regenerated IDL (immediately after the signer) or the instruction fails. Clients using Anchor's IDL-driven resolution need no change — the IDL carries the full PDA derivation including seeds::program, so ban_record resolves automatically. The Rust and TypeScript SDK builders in openfiat-sdks were updated.

Partial deployment is safe in either direction and was not a risk taken blindly: the gate reads an address under the governance program id, so an upgraded escrow/staking/presale simply sees an always-empty address until governance gains list_wallet (every wallet reads as unbanned), and an upgraded governance with un-upgraded enforcers can list a wallet that is not yet refused. banList.devnetProvability: The positive path cannot be exercised on devnet, and this is a property of the deployment rather than of the code. create_proposal transfers deposit_amount (5,000 OPEN) into the deposit vault and cast_vote weighs a real StakeAccount against a quorum of 10% of total_open_supply (100,000,000 OPEN), but the devnet OPEN mint's authority is permanently unset and the genesis buckets holding the supply have unrecoverable keypairs — so no wallet on devnet can fund a proposal or reach quorum. Consequence stated plainly: the devnet ban list is inert in BOTH directions; nothing can be listed and nothing could be delisted. Inert is the safe failure, and zero BanRecord accounts exist so nothing is stranded. The positive path is proven by `anchor test --validator legacy` (92 passing) against a validator with a controllable mint. What IS proven against the deployed binary is the negative that was actually asked for: scripts/prove-devnet-ban-authority.ts runs AS the config admin and shows it cannot list a wallet.

governanceLifecycleEvents.spec: OFS-4100 §9.4 makes on-chain events a hard requirement: without them a participant cannot reconstruct what happened and no explorer can show it. Escrow and staking had 5 event types each; governance had 2 (WalletListed/WalletDelisted), so the entire governance lifecycle — proposals, votes, tallies, deposits — was unobservable.
governanceLifecycleEvents.eightInstructionsThatEmittedNothing: initialize_governance_config -> GovernanceConfigInitialized; update_governance_config -> GovernanceConfigUpdated; create_proposal -> ProposalCreated; cast_vote -> VoteCast; tally_and_finalize -> ProposalFinalized; refund_or_forfeit_deposit -> ProposalDepositSettled; update_config_parameter -> ConfigParameterChangeAuthorized; authorize_treasury_spend -> TreasurySpendAuthorized.
governanceLifecycleEvents.designedForReplayFromLogsAlone: Every event carries the identity an indexer joins on, not just a delta: the Proposal address AND its id, and for a vote the voter, the StakeAccount the weight was read from, and the role. ProposalCreated carries the GovernanceAction in full rather than the ProposalAction address, so a reader deciding how to vote on an exclusion does not have to fetch a second account to learn whom it excludes (OFS-7100 §12.2). The two config events mirror each other field for field, so replaying them in order reconstructs the config's state at any past moment — which is the only way to check that a proposal's quorum/threshold snapshot was taken against the values actually in force.
governanceLifecycleEvents.tallyEmitsQuorumMetNotJustTheOutcome: ProposalFinalized carries votes_for, votes_against, total_cast, both snapshots, quorum_met AND state. quorum_met is a separate fact from acceptance and decides something acceptance does not: refund_or_forfeit_deposit keys on it alone, so a proposal can be rejected on the merits and still have its deposit refunded. An observer who sees only 'Rejected' cannot verify the deposit was handled correctly, and an unverifiable forfeiture is indistinguishable from a confiscation. ProposalDepositSettled then carries refunded AND quorum_met together, redundantly on purpose, so the branch is checkable without joining back to the tally.
governanceLifecycleEvents.castVoteEmitsTheWeightActuallyCounted: VoteCast.weight comes from voter_stake.effective_stake(&staking_config) — the same value added to votes_for/votes_against in the same instruction — and never from anything the voter supplied. cast_vote takes no weight argument at all, so there is nothing self-reported to emit. That is the security property of the whole voting path: crates/rpc's async vote verification exists precisely because a gossiped vote's self-claimed weight cannot be trusted and overrides it with the decoded on-chain stake, and an event echoing a self-reported number would hand every indexer a tally the chain does not agree with. The event also carries voter_stake and role so a reader can refetch that account, apply the same minimum, and arrive at the same number.
governanceLifecycleEvents.theTwoRecordOnlyEventsDoNotImplyAnEffect: update_config_parameter and authorize_treasury_spend set Proposal.executed = true and perform nothing — no parameter is written and no funds move, because the programs they would mutate have no governance-aware authority yet and governance holds no treasury to disburse from (OFS-4200 §1). Their events are named ConfigParameterChangeAuthorized and TreasurySpendAuthorized, with fields authorized_value / authorized_destination / authorized_amount rather than new_value / destination / amount, so an indexer rendering them cannot make them read as a completed change or transfer. The arguments were previously discarded entirely, so an accepted proposal left no on-chain trace of what it had authorized; recording them is the point, implying they took effect would be worse than the silence it replaces. tests/governance.ts asserts the treasury destination's balance is unchanged after the call.
governanceLifecycleEvents.appliedOnDevnet: Governance upgraded IN PLACE at AVJfKUjHsizkGGUy8sdz4Xma2hVgmgvgg8GmUMs8E4eE in 33FuXUnUNHvnwoJVmYJzp6KThrciaF5GpPxHuu8jbfH1NTTk5CF7dpB5xZgzpDGww4urhyCX3uHYdVBK9n7VyBr8. Deployed bytes dumped back and sha256-compared to the tested binary (c8f31e42dc57e24693ae0a37e286932122075046f89cb53bec5781d3e41e985a), exact length with no padding, tail asserted before trimming. The programdata account was auto-extended from 401400 to 414424 bytes to fit. No account layout changed and no migration was needed — events add nothing to any struct.
governanceLifecycleEvents.aFailedFirstAttempt: The first two deploy attempts used --use-rpc and were throttled to a standstill by the public devnet endpoint (HTTP 429), leaving the programdata account extended to 414424 bytes while still holding the OLD 401400-byte binary plus zero padding. Confirmed by dumping and checking that bytes 401400.. were all zero — an extend is not an upgrade, and the program kept working throughout. Dropping --use-rpc (so chunk writes go over TPU instead of the rate-limited RPC) completed in minutes. Dangling buffer accounts from the abandoned attempts were closed and their ~2.9 SOL each reclaimed.

devnet_programs.arbitrationPoolNote: Singleton token account at seeds [arbitration_pool], OPEN-denominated, authority = the FeeConfig PDA so only the escrow program can move it. Created 2026-07-30, sig 1XNXLnsEu88oZXdtCTQkkwFgsdC16JB5xsxFAfcCbCUZpUsmuxmkhoxrDaYBSzWKXPHUksoMqq9Vuw4VxDngWyW. It had never been initialized, and its absence was invisible because only create_liquidity_vault's OPEN carve-out reads it: settlement mints (wSOL/USDC/USDT) worked normally while creating a merchant's OPEN vault failed with ArbitrationPoolNotInitialized, which in turn made charge_ad_listing_fee uncallable and every arbitration deposit zero. The mint is permanent -- the carve-out treats whatever this account holds as the definition of OPEN.

faucet_open_draw.reason: Devnet faucet tooling, NOT an accounting anomaly. OPEN's mint authority is permanently unset, so the devnet faucet cannot mint OPEN the way it mints mock USDC/USDT — the only movable OPEN on devnet is the Community Presale bucket, and the only way out of it is claim() on a Finalized sale. Each draw below is the proceeds of one deliberate, fully-executed presale cycle on its own nonce, run purely to stock the faucet. Nothing was sold and nothing is owed to anyone. Reproduce or audit with scripts/extract-open-for-faucet.ts.
faucet_open_draw.sizing: 10000000 OPEN is 833 grants at the faucet's 12,000 OPEN per-request drip. 12,000 is a deliberate boundary against the live StakingConfig (2wrGGjcUFSn1ZiYzo2o64r7ZC88QNhvvgUYktNs2ifT9): it buys EXACTLY arbitrator + merchant + node operator (10,000 + 1,000 + 1,000) with zero slack. It does NOT cover arbitrator + notification provider (15,000) or all seven roles (20,000) — those need a second grant the next day, since the cap is per 24h. Because 12,000 is exact for that three-role bundle, nothing may be deducted from an OPEN grant for fees or rent; those come out of the faucet's separate SOL grant.
faucet_open_draw.moreAvailable: This is not an irreversible commitment. The presale_vault PDA is a singleton with no nonce, shared by every sale, and initialize_sale only verifies its mint and owner rather than funding it — so any future sale we open as admin reaches the same vault, and topping the faucet up later is one more cycle on a fresh nonce. Add it to DRAWS in the script; do not try to re-open a finalized sale, which is impossible.

devnet_nodes.note: Persistent identities for the docker-compose devnet cluster, living at /data/wallet.json inside each node's volume. Before 2026-07-30 no such file existed, so openfiat-node's load_or_generate_wallet fell through to Wallet::generate() and every node minted a FRESH identity on each boot. That made staking a node impossible in practice: the stake would be stranded against a pubkey that ceased to exist at the next restart. Do not delete these volumes without first unstaking, and keep the keypairs backed up outside the volumes -- node0's key is the only thing that can move its stake.

node0.openSource: faucet stash (10,000,000 -> 9,876,000); OPEN cannot be minted, mint authority is permanently unset

devnet_nodes.stakeNote: node1/node2 sit at exactly the 1,000 OPEN NodeOperator minimum, with zero slack: if StakingConfig.min_stake_by_role[NodeOperator] is ever raised (see the pending 500-floor rework, which lowers rather than raises it, but the point stands) both fall below the floor at once. node0's 100,000 gives the cluster a clear stake-weight leader for exercising SWQoS ranking. All three came from the faucet stash, which cannot be replenished by minting -- OPEN's mint authority is permanently unset.

devnet_presale_claim_anytime_sweep_proof.note: Proves claim-anytime + sweep_proceeds end to end on devnet under a fresh sale_nonce (soft_cap=0). Buyer contributed 60 USDC and claimed 60 OPEN WHILE ACTIVE (no finalize gate); contributed 40 more and a second claim paid only the 40-OPEN delta (claimed_open high-water mark); admin then swept 50 of the 100 USDC in usdc_vault to the fixed treasury while the sale ran, vault 100->50, and a re-read of the buyer OPEN balance AFTER the sweep confirms it is still 100 (claims survive sweeps, proven on-chain post-sweep); the ProceedsSwept event decodes to amount=50000000, vault_remaining=50000000. Program upgraded IN PLACE at 75rJ9. NOTE: an earlier deploy accidentally created a separate program at 97NKN because target/deploy/presale-keypair.json no longer matches declare_id(75rJ9); that junk program was closed (2.4 SOL reclaimed) before the correct in-place upgrade tx above.

devnet_authority_multisig.note: Sub-project 2 part B: the BPF upgrade authority of all four programs (presale, escrow, staking, governance) was migrated from the single EA8Ty keypair to a 3-of-5 Squads v4 multisig on devnet. Proven end to end by scripts/multisig/02-migrate-authorities.ts: a 3-of-5 vote moved SOL from the vault, and escrow was voted from the vault back to EA8Ty (proving the vault wields BPFLoaderUpgradeable SetAuthority and that recovery works) before all four were handed over. Reversible: we hold all five signer keys, so three of them can vote any authority back. The in-program admin/treasury fields (presale.admin/treasury, escrow.admin, staking.admin, governance.admin) are init-only and NOT migratable without a set_admin code change; on mainnet they are initialized directly to the vault. squadsProgram is Squads v4.
